items.title: How much plastic enters the ocean
items.claim: Jambeck et al. (2015, Science) estimated annual plastic input to the oceans from coastal countries. What was the order of magnitude?

options.text: A few hundred tonnes per year
Roughly 4.8-12.7 million tonnes per year (2010 estimate)

items.reveal:
Jambeck et al. (2015) estimated 4.8-12.7 million metric tonnes for 2010. Later estimates (e.g. Borrelle et al., 2020) project rises absent intervention.

The known sinks (surface, beach, deep sea, biota) account for only a fraction of the modelled input, leading to active debate on missing plastic.
items.why: Pollution accounting often produces estimates with wide uncertainty bands but striking headline numbers.

items.title: Ocean pH change since pre-industrial
items.claim: Surface ocean pH has fallen since the late 18th century. By approximately how much?

options.text: About 0.1 units (around 30% rise in hydrogen ion concentration)

items.reveal:
Mean surface ocean pH has declined from around 8.2 to about 8.1 since pre-industrial times. The pH scale is logarithmic, so this is roughly a 26-30% rise in hydrogen ion concentration.

The IPCC SROCC (2019) projected further decline of 0.3-0.4 by 2100 under high-emission scenarios.
items.why: Small numbers on a log scale can correspond to large biological consequences.

items.title: Amazon dieback risk
items.claim: Research from the early 2020s suggests parts of the Amazon may be approaching a tipping point at what threshold of deforestation?
items.reveal:
Lovejoy and Nobre (2018) proposed a tipping point of 20-25% deforestation, combined with climate change, beyond which large parts of the Amazon could shift to savanna.

Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon stood near 17% by 2020 by INPE measurements.
items.why: Ecosystem tipping points have policy salience even when their exact value is uncertain.
